c.tagline: Atlantic island capital of levada walks, wine, and eternal spring.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are yellow with a blue stripe and run on the meter. Uber does not operate on Madeira; Bolt is available but coverage is thin, so pre-booking a taxi or hotel transfer is common.

emergency.note: 112 is the single EU-wide emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The walkable centre around Funchal Cathedral (Sé), the Municipal Square, and the harbour promenade, packed with shops, cafes, and the farmers' market (Mercado dos Lavradores); the most convenient base for first-timers.
The historic Zona Velha of narrow cobbled lanes and painted doors, home to the island's densest cluster of restaurants and bars; best for dining out and nightlife.
A modern seafront district west of the centre with the Lido promenade, sea-bathing complexes, and many of Funchal's larger resort hotels; suits travellers who want the sea on their doorstep.

A cool, green hillside above the city reached by the Teleferico cable car, home to the Monte Palace Tropical Garden and the famous wicker toboggan run; quieter, scenic, and a short bus or taxi from the centre.
A residential and hotel area southwest of the centre near Praia Formosa, Funchal's longest beach, and the Casino/Pestana district; calmer and good value, with easy bus links into town.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.hours: City buses run from roughly 6:00 AM to around 11:00 PM, with limited late-night service; the Monte cable car runs daily until about 6:00 PM.
transit.note: Funchal is served by Horários do Funchal city buses (the yellow buses); there is no metro or tram. The Teleferico do Funchal cable car links the seafront to Monte, from where a traditional wicker toboggan (carro de cesto) slides back downhill.
transit.pay: Pay the driver in cash for single tickets, or tap a rechargeable Giro card for cheaper fares; the Giro card is sold at kiosks and the bus company office.

ferry: Porto Santo Line ferry to Porto Santo island

transit.m: Aerobus / SAM airport bus to Funchal centre (~30-45 min)

tip.r: Service isn't automatically included; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Espetada
food.desc: Chunks of beef rubbed with garlic and bay salt, skewered on a laurel branch and grilled over wood, then hung over the table to drip onto your plate.

places.name: Chalet Vicente
places.note: Old Madeiran house doing wood-grilled espetada; a long-standing local favourite.

places.name: Casa das Espetadas
places.note: Built around the dish, cooked over open wood fires with live music some nights.

places.name: Taberna Ruel
places.note: Old-town tavern with a wood grill and a short, honest Madeiran menu.

food.name: Bolo do caco
food.desc: Round sweet-potato flatbread cooked on a hot basalt stone and split open while hot to be flooded with garlic and parsley butter. Comes with everything.

places.name: Mercado dos Lavradores
places.note: Stalls griddle it in front of you; the cheapest and most casual way to try it.

places.name: Taberna Madeira
places.note: Old-town spot serving it as a starter with proper garlic butter.

places.name: Restaurante Casal da Penha
places.note: Family-run house where bolo do caco arrives before every Madeiran main.

food.name: Lapas grelhadas
food.desc: Limpets prised off the volcanic rocks and grilled in their shells on a metal dish with garlic butter and a squeeze of lemon. Order two rounds.

places.name: Taberna Ruel
places.note: Simple seafood tavern in the old town; limpets arrive sizzling in the pan.

places.name: Taberna Madeira
places.note: Limpets, tuna and octopus done in a relaxed traditional room with a patio.

places.name: Mercado dos Lavradores
places.note: Fish hall restaurants in and around the market cook the morning's shellfish to order.

food.name: Espada com banana
food.desc: Black scabbard fish, a deep-water eel-like creature caught off Madeira, filleted, fried and served with fried banana and passionfruit sauce.

places.name: Restaurante Casal da Penha
places.note: Classic version with banana and passionfruit; long-running family kitchen.

places.name: Gaviao Novo
places.note: Tiny, famously good Rua de Santa Maria fish restaurant; queues form early.

places.name: Taberna Madeira
places.note: Reliable espada plus the rest of the island's fish repertoire.

food.name: Bolo de mel
food.desc: Dark, dense spice cake made with sugar cane honey, walnuts and citrus peel. Traditionally baked in December and broken by hand, never cut with a knife.

places.name: Fabrica Santo Antonio
places.note: Baking the cake by the same recipe since 1893; the shop itself is a period piece.

places.name: Mercado dos Lavradores
places.note: Stalls sell boxed bolo de mel alongside sugar cane honey to take home.

places.name: Restaurante Casal da Penha
places.note: Serves it as dessert with a glass of Madeira, the traditional pairing.

food.name: Milho frito and picado
food.desc: Cubes of set cornmeal fried crisp outside and creamy within, plus picado, garlicky beef bites piled over chips and shared straight from the dish.

places.name: Chalet Vicente
places.note: Picado for the table and proper fried cornmeal alongside the grills.

places.name: Taberna Ruel
places.note: Old-town tavern where picado is the late-night order with a jug of wine.

places.name: Restaurante Casal da Penha
places.note: Milho frito served as a side with almost every Madeiran main course.

food.name: Poncha
food.desc: Sugar cane spirit, honey and citrus juice mashed with a wooden mexelote. Regional means lemon; passionfruit and tangerine versions abound. Deceptively strong.

places.name: Rei da Poncha
places.note: Poncha specialist pouring a range of fruit versions cheaply; also does nikita.

places.name: Rua de Santa Maria bars
places.note: Painted-door street lined with small bars, the easiest poncha crawl in town.

places.name: Taberna da Poncha
places.note: The island's most celebrated poncha shack, worth the short drive inland.

food.name: Madeira wine
food.desc: Fortified wine heated and aged for years, so it never really spoils. Sercial is dry, Malvasia sweet; Verdelho and Bual sit in between. Taste before buying.

places.name: Blandy's Wine Lodge
places.note: Family firm since 1811; tours of the canteiro lofts end with guided tastings.

places.name: D'Oliveiras
places.note: Wonderfully old-fashioned lodge pouring tastes of very old vintages.

places.name: Mercado dos Lavradores
places.note: Stalls open bottles for a taste before you commit to a case.

landmarks: Monte Cable Car (Teleférico do Funchal)
A glass-cabin ride soaring from the old town over terracotta rooftops and banana terraces to the hilltop village of Monte.
Monte Toboggan Run (Carros de Cesto)
Madeira's famous wicker-sledge descent, in which straw-hatted carreiros steer you two kilometers downhill on polished wooden runners.
Monte Palace Tropical Garden
A ravine-filling fantasy garden of koi lakes, azulejo panels, oriental pavilions and one of the world's great cycad collections.
Mercado dos Lavradores
The Art Deco farmers' market bursting with exotic fruit, bird-of-paradise flowers and a tiled fish hall where espada sellers wield black scabbardfish.
Zona Velha and Rua de Santa Maria
The old town's narrow spine, where the Painted Doors art project has turned centuries-old fishermen's houses into an open-air gallery of bars and restaurants.
Sé Cathedral of Funchal
A late-15th-century cathedral from Portugal's Age of Discovery, hiding one of the country's finest Mudéjar-style carved cedar ceilings.
Madeira Botanical Garden
Terraced gardens 300 meters above the bay displaying over 2,000 plant species, geometric flower carpets and sweeping amphitheater views of Funchal.
Fortaleza de São Tiago
A mustard-yellow 17th-century fortress guarding the old town's pebble beach, its ramparts made for photographing the amphitheater city.
Blandy's Wine Lodge
The historic cellars of Madeira's most famous wine dynasty, offering barrel-room tours and tastings of vintages aged for decades in the estufagem heat.
Cabo Girão Skywalk
A glass-floored platform atop one of Europe's highest sea cliffs, suspended 580 dizzying meters above terraced farms and the Atlantic.

train.note: There is no railway on Madeira. The island's only line was the Monte cog railway, which climbed from Funchal to Monte and Terreiro da Luta until it closed in 1943 after a fatal boiler accident; its stone viaducts still stand above the city. Getting up the hill today means the Monte cable car, a bus or a taxi. CP's mainland network (https://www.cp.pt/) has no relevance here.

bus.note: Madeira lies about 500 km off the North African coast, so no bus route can reach it from anywhere. On the island, Horários do Funchal (https://www.horariosdofunchal.pt/) runs the yellow city network from the seafront stops on Avenida do Mar, while Rodoeste covers the west of the island and SAM the east and the airport, both also using Avenida do Mar; the Aerobus airport shuttle runs from the same stretch. Tickets are bought from the driver in cash or loaded onto a Giro card, and rural services thin out sharply at weekends, so check the last return before heading into the mountains.

intl.to: Porto Santo (Portugal) - sails from the Funchal passenger terminal in the harbour, a short walk from the old town

ferry.note: The Lobo Marinho runs Funchal-Porto Santo year-round, covering the 71 km in about 2 hours 15 minutes, typically once a day with extra sailings in summer and an annual maintenance break, so always check the timetable before committing. It leaves from the passenger terminal in Funchal harbour, a few minutes from the cathedral on foot or by taxi, and carries cars, which need booking ahead in July and August. Day-return packages with time ashore on Porto Santo are sold alongside plain crossings, from around EUR 47. There is no longer any scheduled passenger ferry between Madeira and mainland Portugal or the Canary Islands, so the only other way off the island is by air.

half.name: Câmara de Lobos
half.blurb: Colorful fishing village west of Funchal where Winston Churchill once painted, set beneath dramatic cliffside vineyards.

half.name: Curral das Freiras
half.blurb: Village hidden in a deep volcanic crater in Madeira's mountainous interior, reached via a winding switchback road.

half.name: Porto Moniz
half.blurb: Coastal village on Madeira's northwest tip known for natural volcanic-rock swimming pools filled by the Atlantic.

half.name: Pico do Arieiro
half.blurb: Madeira's third-highest peak, offering above-the-clouds views and a trailhead for the ridge hike to Pico Ruivo.
